lesson.title: Two Peaks, Two Populations: Reading Bimodal Data
lesson.summary: A bimodal distribution shows two distinct peaks, usually a sign that the data actually contains two different subgroups that should be examined separately.
lesson.body:
A bimodal distribution has two distinct peaks separated by a noticeable dip, rather than the single smooth hump seen in a unimodal distribution. Just as with unimodal shapes, the count of peaks is a separate question from whether the distribution is symmetric or skewed. A bimodal distribution can be roughly balanced between its two peaks or lopsided, with one peak taller than the other.

The most important reason to care about bimodality is what it usually implies about where the data came from. A single peak generally suggests a single underlying group or process generating fairly consistent values. Two peaks, on the other hand, are a strong visual clue that the data set is really a mixture of two different groups that have been lumped together, each with its own typical value, and that separating them might reveal two much simpler unimodal distributions underneath.

Shoe sizes sold at a shoe store in a single day illustrate this well. Suppose the frequencies by size are: size 6, 1 pair; size 7, 5 pairs; size 8, 2 pairs; size 9, 2 pairs; size 10, 5 pairs; size 11, 1 pair, for 16 pairs total. Plotted as a histogram, the counts rise to a peak of 5 at size 7, dip down to 2 at sizes 8 and 9, then rise back up to a second peak of 5 at size 10 before falling off again. There are two separate local maximums, at size 7 and size 10, with a valley between them, which is exactly the bimodal pattern. In this case the explanation is straightforward: the store sells both women's and men's shoes, and the two peaks correspond to typical sizes for each group combined into a single day's sales data.

Bimodal patterns show up in many everyday contexts once you know to look for them: the arrival times of commuters at a train station often peak once in the morning rush and again in the evening rush, with a lull in between; exam scores in a class can turn bimodal if some students studied the material and others did not, producing one cluster of high scores and one cluster of low scores rather than a smooth spread between them.

One practical caution is worth remembering: a boxplot, which summarizes a distribution using only five landmark numbers, can completely hide a bimodal shape. Two well separated peaks with a gap between them can still produce an ordinary-looking box and pair of whiskers, since a boxplot says nothing about how the data is distributed within each quarter. This is one of the main reasons statisticians insist on examining a histogram or dotplot directly before trusting summary statistics alone, a habit worth carrying through the rest of this course.

When you spot a bimodal shape, the natural next analytical step is to ask what variable might explain the split, whether that is sex, time of day, preparation level, or something else, and to consider examining the two apparent subgroups separately rather than reporting a single mean or median for the whole mixed data set, since a single center-of-distribution number can be misleading when two very different peaks are being averaged together.
